arc: Stage 0 (texts 1-20), November 2026: Olga Ivanova, a nurse in Tallinn, decides to apply for Estonian citizenship. Her Estonian is already B2, so she needs only the exam on the Constitution and the Citizenship Act. Lisa gives her a copy of the Constitution, and the family reads it in the evenings: Lisa helps, Sergei asks practical questions, Nikolai remembers the past, the neighbours Mari and Jaan explain the law and the Riigikogu. Olga registers for the exam.

Stage 1 (texts 21-90), winter 2026/27: rights and freedoms in everyday life. Olga at the hospital, Lisa at school, Sergei at work, Nikolai at home; rights of everyone and rights of citizens only. A young couple from Kharkiv, Maksim and Katja Saar, in Tallinn since 2019, moves into the building. In a box of family papers Maksim finds the Estonian passport of his grandfather Johannes Saar of Tartu, who was an Estonian citizen before 1940. Texts 31-39 are Olga's exam week (6.12-11.12); in text 40 she takes the exam on Saturday 12.12.2026 and passes with 21 of 24; texts 41-45 run to 19.12; texts 46-60 run from 20.12.2026 to 16.01.2027 (Christmas, New Year; Nikolai decides to take the exam; Katja starts selling cakes; the National Archives answers Maksim); texts 61-75 run from 17.01 to 09.02.2027 (Olga fills in her application and books a time at the PPA in March; the birth certificates for Maksim arrive from Kharkiv).

Stage 2 (texts 91-130): citizenship. Olga hands in her application at the PPA in March and gives the oath by signing it (DESIGN.md 4.2); then the waiting and the Government's order. Nikolai starts his own application at 68. Maksim proves his citizenship by birth and gets his first Estonian passport; Katja starts the long road on a residence permit. Side stories: restoration for someone who lost citizenship as a minor, and loss of citizenship.

Stage 3 (texts 131-200): institutions. Jaan's work in the Riigikogu, the President, the Government and the courts, seen through the family's questions. Olga receives her citizenship certificate and her passport.
Stage 4 (texts 201-230): review by area. The family helps Katja prepare for her future exam and quizzes each other in the exam format.

slots.idea: A Tuesday evening in the family's flat in Lasnamäe. Olga tells Lisa that she wants an Estonian passport (Eesti pass); the word kodanik comes later, in text 9. Lisa takes a small blue book from her school bag: Eesti Vabariigi põhiseadus. They read § 1 together: Estonia is an independent and sovereign democratic republic, and the supreme power belongs to the people. Olga repeats the words while she cooks.

Sergei drives a lorry and knows every road. With Olga he looks at the map of Estonia on the kitchen wall: the land, the sea, the islands, Narva and Saaremaa. § 2: the land, waters and airspace are one indivisible whole; Estonia is a unitary state.

On the stairs Olga meets the neighbour Mari, a lawyer at the Chancellor of Justice's office. Mari explains § 3: the state uses its power only on the basis of the Constitution and laws, and only published laws must be followed. She shows Riigi Teataja on her phone.

Dinner at Mari and Jaan's. Jaan, a member of the Riigikogu, explains § 4 with four chairs at the table: the Riigikogu, the President, the Government and the courts. State power is separated and balanced, so no chair rules the others.

Olga writes the first page of a new notebook: republic, the power of the people, the territory, laws, the four institutions. Lisa asks her questions like an examiner, and Olga answers from the notebook.

Saturday in the forest near Tallinn with Olga's father Nikolai. He talks about the trees, the bog and the sea. § 5: the natural wealth and resources of Estonia are national riches that must be used economically.

At the hospital Olga speaks Estonian with an old patient from Tartu (side character in cast, voice albert). § 6: the official language of Estonia is Estonian. The patient praises her Estonian, and Olga says it was hard work.

Lisa paints the blue-black-white flag for a school project. On Sunday the family walks up to Toompea and sees the flag on the Tall Hermann tower. § 7: the national colours of Estonia are blue, black and white.

Mari explains § 56: the people exercise the supreme power through the citizens who have the right to vote, by electing the Riigikogu and in a referendum. Sergei asks why he cannot vote in Riigikogu elections; Mari answers that only citizens do.
The family looks at the photos of the last weeks: the forest, the hospital, the flag on Toompea, the talk about elections. Each photo brings back one §.

Lisa is 16 and asks Jaan when she can vote for the Riigikogu. § 57: Estonian citizens who are 18 vote in Riigikogu elections and referendums. Jaan adds that in local elections citizens of Estonia and of other EU states vote from 16; Lisa was 15 at the last local elections.

Side story. At a petrol station Sergei talks with a colleague (side character in cast, voice albert) whose cousin is in prison. § 58: the law may restrict the voting of citizens whom a court has convicted and who are serving a prison sentence.

Sergei, who has a grey passport, goes to the family doctor. Olga explains that the rights in the Constitution are for everyone in Estonia, also foreigners and stateless people (§ 9), and that everyone is equal before the law (§ 12).

Jaan walks with Olga and Lisa through the old town: the Riigikogu at Toompea castle has the legislative power (§ 59), the President is the head of state (§ 77), the Government in Stenbock House has the executive power (§ 86).
Olga makes flashcards about voting and the institutions, and Lisa tests her on the bus to school.

Lisa tells how she became an Estonian citizen in 2016 as a child of stateless parents: not by birth but by naturalisation. Olga writes four words from § 2 of the Citizenship Act: omandamine, saamine, taastamine, kaotamine. § 8(1) of the Constitution: a child with an Estonian citizen parent has the right to citizenship by birth.
Side story. Lisa's class visits a courtroom in Tallinn; a judge (side character in cast, voice albert) talks to the pupils. § 146: only the courts administer justice, and the courts are independent.

Olga reads the conditions for citizenship in § 6 of the Citizenship Act and ticks them off at the kitchen table: age, years of living in Estonia, Estonian, income, loyalty, the oath. Only one thing is missing: the exam on the Constitution and the Citizenship Act. Lisa helps her register for it in EIS.

Nikolai and Olga talk about loyalty. § 54: a citizen must be loyal to the constitutional order and defend the independence of Estonia. § 55: foreigners and stateless people in Estonia must observe the constitutional order. Olga reads the words of the oath of loyalty.
A quiz evening at home before the next big part, rights and freedoms. Everyone asks Olga one question about texts 16-19, and Nikolai asks the hardest one.

Late November 2026. Maksim and Katja Saar from Kharkiv, in Tallinn since 2019, move into the empty flat on the Ivanovs' floor; Sergei and Lisa help carry boxes. Katja, a Ukrainian citizen on a residence permit, asks whether a foreigner in Estonia has the same rights. Lisa reads § 9: the rights of chapter II apply equally to Estonian citizens and to foreigners and stateless people in Estonia, and (2) to legal persons as far as their nature allows; Maksim's small IT company is a legal person (juriidiline isik). Return § 12: everyone is equal before the law.

slots.idea: Nikolai invites Katja for tea and shows her his old chess set. Katja asks whether a right that the Constitution does not list exists at all. Nikolai reads § 10: the rights listed do not exclude other rights that follow from the spirit of the Constitution or are in accordance with it and with human dignity (inimväärikus) and the principles of a democratic and social state based on the rule of law. Return § 59: legislative power belongs to the Riigikogu.

slots.idea: Flu season at Olga's hospital: visits to the ward are limited (piirang) and a patient's son is angry. At home Mari explains § 11: rights and freedoms may be restricted only in accordance with the Constitution; restrictions must be necessary in a democratic society and must not distort (moonutama) the nature of the rights. Return § 77 as § 77 states it.

slots.idea: Side story in Tartu. A landlord refuses to rent a flat to Leila, a student, because of her religion; her friend Aino, a law student, reads § 12 with her: everyone is equal before the law; no one may be discriminated against on the basis of nationality, race, colour, sex, language, origin, religion, political or other opinion, property or social status, or other circumstances; inciting national, racial, religious or political hatred, violence or discrimination is prohibited and punishable. A hateful comment under Leila's post is the second scene. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md. Return § 86: the Government exercises executive power.

slots.idea: The building's house meeting in the stairwell: the new neighbours Maksim and Katja introduce themselves, and the talk returns to § 9-12: equal rights of citizens and foreigners, rights not listed, how a right may be limited, equality before the law.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Maksim unpacks a box of family papers from Kharkiv and finds the pre-war Estonian passport of his grandfather Johannes Saar of Tartu. Lisa reads § 13: everyone has the right to the protection of the state and the law; the Estonian state protects its citizens abroad too; the law protects everyone against the arbitrariness (omavoli) of state power. Maksim wonders whether he has been a citizen all along. Return § 8(1): a child with an Estonian citizen parent has the right to Estonian citizenship by birth. Nobody is sure yet; Mari will help next time.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Maksim shows Mari his grandfather's passport. Mari reads § 14: guaranteeing rights and freedoms is the duty of the legislative, executive and judicial powers and of local governments (omavalitsus). Then KodS § 2 (return): citizenship is acquired by birth, received by naturalisation, restored, or lost; Maksim's case would be acquisition by birth, so he takes no exam. Mari tells him he will need a National Archives (Rahvusarhiiv) certificate and the birth certificates; no promise of a result yet.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Sergei, a driver, gets a city decision he thinks is wrong (a parking fine from the city of Tallinn on his work van). Mari reads § 15: everyone whose rights and freedoms are violated has the right to go to court; in a case, a person may ask the court to declare unconstitutional any law, other legal act or measure that is relevant to the case. Return § 146: only courts administer justice, and they are independent. Olga worries about money; Sergei decides to complain first and go to court if needed.

slots.idea: Side story in Pärnu in early December. A paramedic, Svetlana, and her partner save a fisherman who fell through the ice; nobody asks who he is or what colour his skin is (nahavärvus). § 16: everyone has the right to life, protected by law, and no one may be arbitrarily deprived of life. Return KodS § 6: Svetlana is stateless and ticks off the conditions of naturalisation, like Olga. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: The Saars' housewarming in early December. Each guest brings a small gift and a question about § 13-16: protection of the state and law, who guarantees rights, going to court, the right to life. Sergei tells how his fine ended; Maksim says he has written to the National Archives. Olga's exam is close.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Sunday 6.12, evening. On her phone screen (ekraan) Lisa sees a drawing in her gymnasium class chat: Robin, a classmate who lives on the fifth floor of their building, has drawn (joonistama) Lisa copying her essay from the internet and written that she cheated. It is not true: Lisa is not guilty (süüdi olema). She shows it to Olga and Nikolai. Nikolai reads § 17: no one's honour (au) or good name (hea nimi) may be defamed (teotama). Olga tells Lisa not to answer with a mean drawing of her own; on Monday Lisa will talk to her class teacher. Return § 54: Lisa is a citizen, and § 54(1) says a citizen's duty is to be loyal (ustav) to the constitutional order and to defend Estonia's independence; Nikolai adds that § 17 binds everyone, not only citizens, so Robin's honour must not be defamed either. Six days to Olga's exam. Do not invent consequences for Robin (no penalty, no court, no police): the story stays with the § text.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Monday 7.12. At the hospital a doctor asks an elderly patient whether he wants to join a study of a new medicine; the study needs the required number (vajalik arv) of patients. The patient hesitates, and Olga tells him he may say no: § 18(2): no one may be subjected to medical or scientific experiments against his or her free will. In the evening Katja and Maksim come for tea; Olga tells the story without the patient's name (a nurse keeps it secret). Katja reads § 18(1): no one may be tortured, treated (kohtlema) cruelly or in a degrading way, or punished (karistama) so. Katja asks whether foreigners have duties too: Maksim reads § 55: citizens of other states and stateless persons in Estonia must observe Estonia's constitutional order (järgima põhiseaduslikku korda); Katja: that means me, and Olga and Sergei too. Maksim says that if the National Archives confirms it, his case is acquisition of citizenship by birth (kodakondsuse omandamine sünniga); there is no answer yet. Do not say whether Maksim keeps his Ukrainian citizenship.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Monday night 7.12 to Tuesday morning 8.12. Olga studies for Saturday's exam, but through the wall comes Maksim's electric guitar; he dreams of becoming a famous (kuulus) guitarist, his free self-realisation (vaba eneseteostus). Tuesday morning on the stairs Olga talks to Maksim and Katja. Katja reads § 19: (1) everyone has the right to free self-realisation (eneseteostus); (2) in exercising (kasutamine) their rights and freedoms and in performing (täitmine) their duties, everyone must respect and consider (arvestama) the rights and freedoms of others and observe the law. They agree among themselves: guitar until 21:00, then headphones (a neighbours' agreement, not a rule of law: do not state any legal quiet hours). Olga tells them about her own road, receiving citizenship by naturalisation (kodakondsuse saamine naturalisatsiooni korras), and the exam on Saturday. Return § 9: the rights of chapter II, § 19 among them, apply equally to Estonian citizens and to foreigners and stateless persons in Estonia.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Side story in Narva on a winter night. A police officer, Kadri, patrols with a young colleague, Mihkel. First Mihkel wants to take a man walking home to the station because he 'looks strange'. Kadri stops him: § 20(1): everyone has the right to liberty and security of person (isikupuutumatus), and liberty may be taken only in the cases and by the procedure the law sets (§ 20(2)). Later a call: someone has broken a kiosk window and runs away; they catch him. Now he is reasonably suspected of a crime (kuritegu, kahtlustatav); § 20(2) p 3 allows taking liberty to prevent a crime or an administrative offence (haldusõiguserikkumine, a kind of õiguserikkumine), to bring a person reasonably suspected of one before the competent state body (pädev riigiorgan), or to prevent his escape (pakkuminek). Kadri says the police officer performs her duties (kohustusi täitma) within the law. Return § 10: rights not listed in chapter II still exist when they follow from the spirit of the Constitution and accord with human dignity (inimväärikus); Kadri speaks politely to the suspect. Do not invent procedure (no hours, no court steps, no penalties). Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Summary of § 17-20. Tuesday evening 8.12: the family bakes gingerbread (piparkoogid) for Christmas with Katja. Lisa writes § numbers on the cookies with icing: 17 on a heart (honour and good name: Robin apologised to Lisa on Monday), 18 on a star (no cruel or degrading treatment; no medical experiment against one's free will: Olga's patient, no name), 19 on a guitar (free self-realisation and respecting others: Maksim now plays until 21:00), 20 on a key (everyone has the right to liberty and security of person; liberty may be taken only in the cases and by the procedure the law sets). A table (tabel) on the fridge counts the days to Olga's exam on Saturday 12.12: four days. The family has not met the Narva police officers of text 34 and does not mention them.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Wednesday 9.12, Olga's last long shift before the exam. A patient with a dangerous infectious disease (nakkushaige) wants to go home and could infect his family. The doctor (side character) explains that § 20(2) p 5 allows the detention (kinnipidamine) of an infectious patient, a mentally ill person (vaimuhaige), an alcoholic (alkohoolik) or a drug addict (narkomaan) when he is dangerous (ohtlik olema) to himself or to others, and only in the cases and by the procedure the law sets; he talks to the patient, who agrees to stay. Do not invent the procedure (no court, no hours). In the evening Lisa quizzes Olga on § 20(2): p 3 (a crime or administrative offence; the words kuritegu, kahtlustatav, pädev riigiorgan are known from text 34), p 4 (a minor, alaealine, and educational supervision, kasvatuslik järelevalve: Lisa jokes that she is a minor but nobody supervises her homework), p 5 (the hospital case). Points 1, 2 and 6 come in text 37: do not use their words here. Return § 11: rights may be restricted only in accordance with the Constitution, and the restrictions must be necessary in a democratic society; Olga remembers the visiting restriction in the flu season (text 23). Lisa says the Constitution speaks of the rights of all and everyone (kõigi ja igaühe õigused). Side character in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Thursday 10.12. Two worries for Sergei. First a letter from the city of Tallinn about his parking fine (texts 28, 30): his complaint is accepted, the sign was under snow, and he does not have to pay; he did not need the court. Return § 12: everyone is equal before the law, and the city looked at his complaint like anyone's. Second: Sergei bought a washing machine on instalments, a contract with a shop, and this month he had fewer shifts, so he cannot pay on time. He jokes nervously: will they put him under arrest (arest)? Lisa reads § 20(2) p 1: liberty may be taken to carry out a convicting (süüdimõistev) court judgment (kohtuotsus) or an arrest set (määrama) by a court; and § 20(3): no one may be deprived of liberty solely (üksnes) because he is unable to fulfil a contractual obligation (lepinguline kohustus). Olga: still, he must keep his word and call the shop to agree on a later date. Lisa also reads p 6, preventing illegal settling in Estonia (ebaseaduslik Eestisse asumine) and expulsion or extradition; Sergei: not about him, he lives in Estonia permanently (püsivalt) and legally, with a residence permit (elamisluba). Do not invent what the shop or a court may do about the debt. Two days to the exam.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Friday 11.12, the evening before the exam. Mari comes to wish Olga luck; she has come straight from work, where today she visited a police arrest house (arestimaja). She quizzes Olga on § 21(1): everyone deprived of liberty is told immediately (viivitamatult), in a language and manner he understands, the reason for taking (võtmine) his liberty and his rights, and gets the chance to tell his close relatives; a person suspected of a crime also gets, immediately, the chance to choose a defence counsel (kaitsja) and to meet him; the suspect's right to tell his relatives may be restricted only in the cases and by the procedure the law sets, to prevent a crime or in the interests of establishing (väljaselgitamine) the truth (tõde) in criminal proceedings (kriminaalmenetlus). Katja asks whether a detained person who speaks no Estonian is told in Russian or Ukrainian: in a language he understands (§ 21(1)). Mari also previews § 21(2): no one may be held in custody (vahi all) for more than 48 hours without the court's permission (ilma loata), and the court's decision is told to the arrested person (vahistatu) immediately. Return § 13: everyone has the right to the protection of the state and the law, and the law protects everyone against the arbitrariness of state power. Olga: tomorrow she does not have to (ei pea) know everything by heart, but she knows a lot. Do not state what Mari's office is legally entitled to do.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Side story in Tartu. A student, Marten, is detained on Friday night outside a bar as a person suspected of a crime (kuriteos kahtlustatav) after a fight; he says he only pulled the fighters apart. The fight began when one man shouted insults about another man's race (rass); his defence counsel Anu says § 12 forbids inciting racial hatred. Anu meets Marten at the police station and explains § 21(2): no one may be held in custody for more than 48 hours without the court's permission, and the court's decision is told to the arrested person immediately in a language and manner he understands. Marten, an Estonian citizen by birth, is afraid he could lose his citizenship (kodakondsuse võtmine); Anu: § 8(3), no one may be deprived of Estonian citizenship acquired by birth. On Sunday, before 48 hours have passed, the court does not give permission to keep him in custody, and his mother takes him home. Return § 14: guaranteeing rights and freedoms is the duty of the legislative, executive and judicial powers and of local governments. Do not invent procedure beyond § 21 (no prosecutor steps, no penalties). Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Summary of § 20-21 on the exam day, Saturday 12.12. Sergei drives Olga to the exam centre in Tallinn; Lisa and Nikolai come along and wait in a café. Use only these facts about the exam (DESIGN.md 2.1): 24 questions in Estonian, 45 minutes, on a computer; the texts of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act and a dictionary are available; at least (vähemalt) 18 correct answers pass; the result is shown right after the exam. In the quiet (vaikne) hall (saal) Olga reads the questions. Two of them are about this week: § 20 (liberty may be taken only in the cases and by the procedure the law sets; not solely for a contract debt) and § 21 (the reason told in a language he understands; 48 hours without the court's permission). One question is difficult (keeruline), and she checks (kontrollima) it in the law text. Result on the screen: 21 of 24, passed. The family celebrates. The next step, the application to the PPA, is for later: no details, no dates, no fee. Do not describe anything else about the exam (no ID rules, no room rules, no certificate).
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Sunday 13.12. Maksim's bicycle has disappeared from the stairwell. An older neighbour, Mr Tamm (side character), says it was surely Robin from the fifth floor, the boy with long hair (juus): he is a thief! Lisa, though Robin drew the mean picture of her a week ago (text 31), defends him. Mari reads § 22: (1) no one may be treated (käsitama) as guilty of a crime before a convicting court judgment against him has entered into force (jõustuma); (2) no one is obliged (kohustatud olema) in criminal proceedings to prove (tõendama) his innocence (süütus); (3) no one may be compelled (sundima) to testify against himself or his close relatives. Robin's honour (au) must not be defamed (teotama) either: § 17. In the evening the bicycle turns up: Jaan had carried it to the basement to clean the stairs; Mr Tamm apologises to Robin. Return § 15: everyone whose rights are violated may go to court; Maksim says nobody needs a court over a bicycle. The neighbours congratulate Olga on passing her exam (eksam) yesterday. Robin does not need to speak. Side character in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Tuesday 15.12, evening. Jaan comes home late from Toompea Castle (loss), where the Riigikogu sits, and plays chess with Nikolai on Nikolai's old chess set (text 22); Lisa watches. Jaan says a new bill was discussed today; it has no name and no party, and nobody gives an opinion about it. Nikolai asks whether a new law can punish what someone did before it. Jaan: § 23(1): no one may be convicted of an act if a law in force (jõus) at the time did not make it a crime; (2) no one may be given a heavier punishment than the one that could be imposed when the offence was committed, and if a law passed after the offence sets a lighter punishment, the lighter one applies (kohaldama); (3) no one may be tried or punished a second time for an act of which he has been finally (lõplikult) convicted or acquitted in accordance with (vastavalt) the law. Nikolai remembers (mäletama) a personal, non-political moment of his youth (noorus), for example a football match whose rules changed after the game. Nikolai wins (võitma) the game (mäng). Return § 16 in a fact or a question (everyone has the right to life, protected by law). Jaan may mention that the next Riigikogu elections are in 2027 (valimine), with no opinions.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Thursday 17.12. Olga, free after the exam, takes Katja and Nikolai on an excursion (ekskursioon) to the Tallinn courthouse, where Lisa's class was in text 17. At the door Nikolai asks whether anyone may come in: § 24(3): court sessions (istung) are public (avalik). The case: a café owner says a blogger defamed his honour and good name with false reviews (back to § 17); both are in the courtroom, because § 24(2) gives everyone the right to be present at the hearing of his case. When the café's figures come up, the judge, Mr Lepp from text 17, declares that part of the session closed (kinnine) to protect a business secret (ärisaladus), and the three leave the hall. Outside Olga reads the rest of § 24(3): a court may close its session in the cases and by the procedure the law sets (seaduses sätestatud korras), to protect a state or business secret, morals (kõlblus), or family and private life (eraelu), or when the interests of a minor, a victim or the administration of justice (õigusemõistmine) require it. Katja asks whether a case could be moved to another court: § 24(1): no one may be transferred against his free will from the jurisdiction (alluvus) of the court the law sets to another court. The judgment will come later and will be public (avalik kohtuotsus): that is § 24(4), the next text. Return § 17 in a fact or a question.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Side story in Pärnu. Kertu, a young court reporter for a local newspaper, spends a day at the courthouse (kohtuistung). In the first case a man is convicted of stealing boats in the winter harbour; the boat owner, the victim (kannatanu), is in the courtroom, and the judgment is announced publicly. The man says he will appeal (edasi kaebama, kaebama) to a higher court (kõrgemalseisev kohus); § 24(5): everyone has the right to appeal against a court decision about him to a higher court by the procedure the law sets. In the afternoon her editor wants a story about a well-known couple's divorce; in that case the judgment is not announced publicly, because the interests of a spouse (abielupool) require otherwise (§ 24(4): judgments are announced publicly except when the interests of a minor, a spouse or a victim require otherwise). Kertu writes no names and respects their private life. Return § 18 in a fact or a question. Do not invent which court hears the appeal or any deadline. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Summary of § 22-24. Saturday 19.12: the Christmas market on Town Hall Square (Raekoja plats) in the Old Town; the Ivanovs and the Saars celebrate Olga's passed exam with hot drinks and gingerbread. Each recalls a scene of the week: Robin and the bicycle (§ 22: no one is treated as guilty before a convicting judgment enters into force; no one has to prove his innocence; no one may be compelled to testify against himself or his close relatives), Jaan and Nikolai's chess (§ 23: no punishment for an act that was not a crime under the law in force at the time; the lighter punishment applies; not twice for the same act), the court excursion (§ 24: public sessions, closed for a business secret; the right to be present; the right to appeal to a higher court). Maksim still has no answer from the National Archives. Olga's next step is the application to the PPA: no details or dates.
slots.grammar: past tense, clauses with et and kui

slots.idea: Sunday 20.12, a shopping centre in Tallinn, Christmas presents. The shop alarm rings as Lisa walks out; a security guard (side character) shouts that she is a thief and pulls her bag in front of everyone. The zip breaks, her phone falls and its screen (ekraan) cracks. The alarm was faulty: a shop assistant had left a tag on the scarf Olga had just paid for. The manager (side character) apologises and offers to pay for the screen. At home Lisa reads § 25: everyone has the right to compensation (hüvitamine) for moral (moraalne) and material (materiaalne) damage caused to him or her unlawfully by anyone (materiaalne kahju: the screen; moral damage: the shame in front of people). The § says 'by anyone', not only by the state. Return § 19: in exercising rights everyone must respect the rights of others; the guard should have checked first. The story does not decide whether the guard acted unlawfully, says nothing about security-guard law, insurance or amounts, and says only that the shop agreed to pay for the screen. The phrase maa-ala (territory) may appear naturally, for example in a remark about Estonia's territory. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.

So Andris has this right too, unless the law says otherwise. Use ühiskonnakiht naturally (for example: people from every social stratum come to the town government with questions). The story does not say what the data are or how long the answer takes. Side characters in cast, voices per docs/writing-texts.md.
